name: Habakkuk
sourceNote:
Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text). It was checked against several other witnesses:
- The Habakkuk Commentary (Pesher Habakkuk, 1QpHab) from Qumran Cave 1, copied in the late 1st century BC. It quotes Habakkuk 1–2 phrase by phrase and differs from the Masoretic Text at several points.
- The Hebrew Minor Prophets scroll from Wadi Murabba‘at (MurXII, early 2nd century AD).
- The Septuagint, using Brenton’s public-domain English translation.
The scroll readings come from Martin Abegg’s transcriptions, as published in the ETCBC Dead Sea Scrolls dataset. Portions of Habakkuk also survive in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr, about the turn of the era), a revision of the Septuagint toward the Hebrew. Its readings could not be checked directly and are marked “reported.” Significant differences are footnoted; differences of spelling and damage to the scrolls are not. The divine title YHWH Tseva’ot is translated “Yahweh of Armies” (see the note at 2:13). Poetry is printed line by line.

verses.text: The oracle that Habakkuk the prophet saw.{a}

Yahweh, how long must I plead for help
while you refuse to listen?
I shout to you, “Violence!”
yet you do not rescue.

Why do you make me see iniquity,
and why do you look upon trouble?
Ruin and violence are before me;
there is strife, and contention arises.

“Look among the nations, and see;{b}
be astonished and amazed!
For I am doing a work in your days
that you would not believe if it were told.

For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans,{c}
that bitter and impetuous nation,
which marches through the breadth of the earth
to seize dwellings that are not its own.

It is dreadful and fearsome;
its justice and its dignity go forth from itself.

At kings they scoff,
and rulers are a laughingstock to them.
They laugh at every fortress,
for they heap up earth and capture it.

Then they sweep on like the wind and pass by,
and become guilty, they whose own strength is their god.”{e}

Your eyes are too pure to look upon evil,
and you cannot gaze upon wrong.
Why then do you look on the treacherous{g}
and keep silent when the wicked swallows up
one more righteous than he?

You make mankind like the fish of the sea,
like creeping things that have no ruler.

Therefore he sacrifices to his net
and burns incense to his dragnet;
for by them his portion is rich
and his food is plentiful.

Shall he therefore keep emptying his net,{h}
and slaying nations continually without pity?

notes.text: “Oracle”: Hebrew massa’, which can also mean “burden.” The meaning of the name Habakkuk is uncertain. It may come from a Hebrew root meaning “embrace,” or it may be related to the Akkadian name of a garden plant (hambaququ).

The Septuagint has “Behold, you despisers,” apparently reading bogedim (“traitors, the treacherous”) for baggoyim (“among the nations”). Acts 13:41 quotes the verse in that form. The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran (1QpHab) quotes the line as “among the nations,” as the Masoretic Text has it. Its commentary, however, applies the passage to “the traitors.”
The Chaldeans were the Neo-Babylonian dynasty and its people. They overthrew Assyria and conquered Judah, taking Jerusalem in 597 and 586 BC.
The Hebrew phrase translated “the set of their faces” is obscure.
Literally “and he shall be guilty, he whose strength is his god.” The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran reads “and he makes his strength his god” (wayyasem instead of we’ashem).

According to an ancient Jewish tradition, this is one of the places where the scribes altered the wording out of reverence, and the original was “You shall not die.” The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran and the Septuagint both read “we.”
The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran has a plural, “Why do you look on, you treacherous ones?”
The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran reads “Therefore he keeps drawing his sword” (harbo, instead of hermo, “his net”).

verses.text:
Shall not all these take up a taunt against him,
with mocking riddles about him, and say,
“Woe to him who multiplies what does not belong to him—
how long?—
and makes himself heavy with pledges!”

Shall not those who bite you rise up in a moment,
and those wake who shake you violently?
And you shall become plunder to them.

Because you plundered so many nations,
the rest of the peoples will plunder you,
for human bloodshed and violence to the land,
to cities and everyone who lives in them.

Woe to him who gets evil gain for his house,
to set his nest on high,
to be delivered from the grasp of evil!

For out of the wall the stone shall cry,
and out of the timber the rafter shall answer it.

Doom to the man who constructs a town by murder
and establishes a city on injustice!

You will be sated with shame instead of glory.
Drink, you also, and be exposed as uncircumcised!{j}
The cup in Yahweh’s right hand will come around to you,
and utter disgrace will be upon your glory.

What profit is an idol
when its maker has carved it,
a molten image and a teacher of falsehood,
that the one who shapes it should trust in what he has shaped,
making idols that cannot speak?

Woe to him who says to a piece of wood, “Wake up!”
or to a mute stone, “Arise!”
Can this teach?
Behold, it is plated with gold and silver,
and there is no breath at all within it.

But Yahweh is in his holy temple;
let all the earth keep silence before him.

notes.text: Or “concerning my reproof.”
Or “so that a herald may run with it.”
Hebrews 10:37 quotes verses 3–4 in their Septuagint form. Compare “the end” here with 2 Peter 3:9.

Or “by his faith.” Hebrew be’emunato: ’emunah is steadfastness, faithfulness, and trust. The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran quotes the line as it stands in the Masoretic Text, and its commentary applies it to those whom God will deliver “because of their toil and their faith in the Teacher of Righteousness.” The Septuagint reads “by my faith” (or “by my faithfulness,” meaning God’s). Some Septuagint manuscripts read “my righteous one shall live by faith,” the form that Hebrews 10:38 follows. The Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever is reported to read “by his faith,” agreeing with the Hebrew. Paul quotes the line, without a pronoun, in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11.
The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran reads “wealth (hon) is treacherous” instead of “wine (hayyayin).” The Septuagint has “the arrogant man and the scorner.”
Sheol is the realm of the dead, the grave.
Compare Isaiah 11:9.
Hebrew YHWH Tseva’ot, traditionally “the LORD of hosts.” The “armies” are the forces of heaven (the angels and the stars) and sometimes the armies of Israel.

The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran reads “to look upon their festivals” (mo‘adehem instead of me‘orehem, “their nakedness”). Its commentary applies the verse to an attack by “the Wicked Priest” on the Teacher of Righteousness on the Day of Atonement.

The Hebrew he‘arel means “show your foreskin, be exposed as uncircumcised.” The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran reads hera‘el, “and stagger,” with two letters reversed. The Septuagint (“shake… and quake”) and other ancient versions point the same way, and many translations follow that reading.
“Will terrify you” follows the Septuagint. The Masoretic Text has a form usually read as “will terrify them,” and the Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran has another spelling of the word.

verses.text: A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, according to Shigionoth.{a}

God came from Teman,
the Holy One from Mount Paran. Selah{c}
His glory blanketed the skies,
and the earth overflowed with his praise.

Pestilence went before his face,
and plague went out at his feet.{e}

Under affliction I saw the tents of Cushan;{g}
the curtains of Midian’s land were shaking.

Was Yahweh angry with the rivers?
Was your anger against the rivers,
or your fury against the sea,
when you rode upon your horses,
your chariots of salvation?

Sun and moon stood still in their dwelling
at the light of your arrows as they flew,
at the gleam of your flashing spear.

In fury you strode over the earth;
in wrath you threshed the nations.

You went forth for the salvation of your people,
for the salvation of your anointed.
You crushed the head of the house of the wicked,
laying bare the foundation to the neck. Selah

You trampled the sea with your horses,
the heaving of many waters.

yet I will rejoice in Yahweh;
I will exult in the God of my salvation.

notes.text: Shigionoth is probably a musical or liturgical term. Its meaning is unknown; compare the title of Psalm 7. The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran comments only on chapters 1–2.
The Septuagint has a very different text here, beginning “You shall be known between the two living creatures.”

Teman (in Edom) and Mount Paran (in the Sinai peninsula) lie to the south of Judah. Compare Deuteronomy 33:2 and Judges 5:4. Selah is a term of uncertain meaning, probably musical or liturgical; it occurs here and in verses 9 and 13.
Hebrew qarnayim, literally “horns,” used here of rays of light.
Hebrew dever (“pestilence”) and reshef (“plague, burning fever”). Reshef is also the name of a Canaanite god of plague, and here it may picture plague as one of God’s attendants.
Or “and shook the earth.”
Cushan appears only here. It may be a poetic name for Cush, or the name of a tribe connected with Midian (compare Numbers 12:1).
The Hebrew of this line is notoriously obscure. Literally it is “sworn were the rods (or tribes) of the word.”
The Wadi Murabba‘at Minor Prophets scroll reads “the clouds poured out water,” as in Psalm 77:17. The Masoretic Text has “the torrent of waters swept by.”
The Hebrew of verse 14 is difficult, and the translation is uncertain.
Hebrew YHWH Adonai. “My high places” are the heights.
This note is addressed to the leader of the temple music, like the titles of many psalms.
